# The Thirty-Seven Letters of Monk Hideo, As Compiled by His Opponent

---

## Editor's Preface

The letters contained in this volume were sent to me over a period of forty-one years, beginning in the autumn of 1961 and concluding in the spring of 2002. They are presented in chronological order as received, with dates of receipt noted where postmarks were legible. Where the postmark was damaged or absent, I have estimated the date based on internal references to season, festival, or monastic calendar. I have not corrected Hideo's occasional errors of grammar or calligraphy. I have not censored, excerpted, or rearranged. These are his letters, whole, as they reached me.

Hideo Takashi is known to readers of this country's martial history as the finest kendōka of the postwar generation, and perhaps of any generation. His record in national and international competition between 1949 and 1961 is a matter of public documentation and requires no elaboration here. What requires elaboration — what has generated four decades of speculation, rumor, hagiography, and lie — is the single act by which he departed that record: his withdrawal from the final match of the 1961 All Japan Kendo Championships, a match he was favored to win, and his subsequent disappearance into monastic life at the age of thirty-four. I was his opponent that day.

In the years since, I have been asked by journalists, historians, students, and strangers on trains to explain why Hideo forfeited. I have not answered because I was not given an answer. These letters, which I believe constitute the most sustained private writing by any figure of Hideo's stature, may or may not contain one. I present them as a scholarly service. I present them because the historical record requires it. I present them because I am seventy-seven years old and in what my physician describes, with his profession's gift for understatement, as "declining health," and these letters should not leave the world when I do.

I have held these letters longer than I have held anything, including my own reasons for holding them.

A note on the annotations: I have added brief contextual notes where I judged them necessary for comprehension. They are factual in nature and offered in the spirit of editorial responsibility. They are not memoir.

Fujimoto Kenji
Yokohama, November 2003

---

## I. The Forfeit

### From the Mainichi Shimbun, November 12, 1961

> In the most shocking conclusion to a national championship in the sport's modern history, Hideo Takashi, the three-time defending champion who had not lost a competitive match in six years, bowed to his opponent, removed his *men*, and walked from the floor of the Nippon Budōkan without striking or receiving a single blow. No explanation was offered to officials. Fujimoto Kenji, the opposing finalist, remained at his mark. The crowd, numbering approximately three thousand, sat in what this reporter can only describe as a communal paralysis for eleven minutes before arena staff began to guide spectators toward the exits. Hideo could not be reached for comment. He was seen boarding a train at Tokyo Station shortly after two o'clock. His coach, Mori Yoshitaka, told reporters: "I have nothing to say because I have nothing to understand."

---

### From Letter No. 3 (received February 1962)

> …and what I remember is not what you will expect me to remember. I remember the sound of my sandals in the corridor. Cork-soled, the pair I had worn through all three championships, and they made a sound on the polished concrete that was like — this will seem foolish — like a man clicking his tongue against the roof of his mouth. Click, click, click. Very regular. I was walking at a pace that I recognized later as the pace I used during morning meditation walks at my teacher's house in Fuchu. Not hurried. Not slow. The pace of a man who has somewhere to be. The corridor opened onto the service entrance, and I remember the quality of the November light, which was the pale gray of a television screen before the picture arrives. The attendant at the door was eating a rice ball. He did not recognize me without the *bōgu*. I said "excuse me" and he shifted his knees to let me pass, and I walked out into the air, which tasted of exhaust and the particular sweetness of ginkgo rot. From the Budōkan to Tokyo Station is approximately twenty-five minutes on foot if one is not delayed by traffic signals. I was delayed by two. I stood at each one and watched the lights cycle and felt nothing unusual, only the ordinary patience of a pedestrian. The platform was crowded. I stood behind a woman carrying a child in a yellow coat. The child looked at me with the suspicion that children reserve for adults whose faces are doing something unexpected, though I was not aware my face was doing anything at all.

*Editor's note: He describes the weather. He describes the sound of his sandals on gravel. He does not describe what I saw in his eyes when he bowed.*

---

## II. The Early Letters

Letters one through six, spanning December 1961 through August 1964, are presented here in summary. The full texts are reproduced in Appendix A for readers who wish to examine them in their entirety. I summarize for reasons of economy, and because the early letters share a quality of surface that makes individual examination less productive than a view of the whole.

The first letter arrived seven weeks after the championship. It was brief. Hideo thanked me for "a career of worthy opposition" and informed me that he had taken vows at a monastery in Fukui Prefecture. He asked that I not share this information. He inquired about my students. He wished me good health. He signed the letter with the formal *keigu* closing.

I did not reply.

The second letter arrived four months after the first. It described the monastic day in some detail: waking at three-forty in the morning, seated meditation until five, chanting, cleaning, breakfast of rice gruel and pickled radish. He noted the taste of the barley tea ("more smoke than barley, as though someone has brewed a small fire"). He described the rain on the cedar shingles of the meditation hall as sounding "like a crowd whispering a single word, over and over, that you cannot quite distinguish." He asked after my students again, by name. He recommended a particular sequence of wrist exercises for Tanaka, my most promising junior, whose *kote* strikes he had apparently been observing at regional tournaments for years.

*Editor's note: The temple he references is Eiheiji. The wrist exercise he describes is standard.*

The third letter contained the passage about the walk from the Budōkan, excerpted above. Beyond this passage, the letter discussed the monastic practice of *samu*, or working meditation, and the difficulty of learning to sweep a wooden floor without treating the broom as an instrument. "The abbot tells me I am still fighting the dust," he wrote. "He says I hold the broom as though it has weight. I am trying to learn to hold it as though it has none."

The fourth letter, nearly a year after the third, was the shortest of the entire correspondence: six lines inquiring about the health of my wife, whom he had met once, briefly, at a tournament reception in 1957. He remembered that she had been wearing "a blue dress with small white flowers, or possibly white with small blue flowers" and that she had said something kind to him about his footwork that she could not have understood technically, which made the kindness, in his view, "more pure."

*Editor's note: My wife confirmed that the dress was white with blue flowers. She passed away in 1998. I did not inform Hideo.*

The fifth letter described the monastery's garden in winter. The sixth described it in spring. Both letters were pleasant, observant, and conventional. Both asked after my students. Neither mentioned kendo except in the most incidental way — a reference to the posture required during hours of seated meditation ("not unlike the settled readiness of *chūdan no kamae*, though directed at nothing, or possibly at everything"), a passing note about a young monk whose movements during walking meditation reminded Hideo of a kendōka he had once watched at a prefectural tournament in Niigata.

He signed each letter with warmth and formality. He expressed hope that I was well. He said nothing at all about why he had walked off the floor of the Nippon Budōkan and out of his life, and I, who had not replied to any of these letters, said nothing in return.

---

## III. The Philosophical Letters

I do not know precisely when the shift occurred, because the letters do not change suddenly. It is more as though a tide came in while I was not watching the waterline. Letters seven and eight, which I do not reproduce in full, are recognizably continuous with the earlier correspondence: temple life, weather, polite inquiry. But by letter nine, received in the early months of 1969, the texture has altered. The letters grow longer. They become less interested in the world Hideo inhabits and more interested in the world he carries.

---

### Letter No. 9 (received March 1969, postmark partially illegible)

Fujimoto,

I have been given a text to study — you will forgive me for not naming it, as the assignment was given in the context of my practice, and I do not wish to treat what is sacred as what is merely interesting — that concerns the obligations of a man who perceives a truth that another man does not perceive about himself. The text is Buddhist in origin, but the problem is, I think, universal, and I find my thoughts turning to it during hours when I should be turning to nothing.

Let me pose it as a question, stripped of its religious clothing:

If a man is standing in a house, and you can see from outside that the house is burning, but the man inside feels no heat and smells no smoke — do you shout? Common sense says yes. But what if the man has built this house himself, and it is the only house he has ever lived in, and your shouting will not save the house but will only ensure that the man's last moments in it are filled with terror rather than peace? What then? Is your silence a kindness or a cowardice? And if the house is not a house but a body — if what is burning is not a structure but a self — does the calculus change?

I do not know why I write these questions to you. Possibly because you are the only person I have known who would refuse to answer them quickly.

The cherry trees behind the meditation hall bloomed early this year. The abbot says it is because of the warm February. I say it is because the trees have no interest in our calendars.

With respect,
Hideo

*Editor's note: I was unable to identify the source text he references. The cherry trees at Eiheiji bloom, on average, in mid-April. In 1969, February temperatures in Fukui Prefecture were 2.3 degrees above the seasonal norm.*

---

### Letter No. 10 (received September 1969)

Fujimoto,

I have been thinking further about what I wrote in my last letter, and I find that my analogy was imprecise, which means my thinking was imprecise, which means I have wasted your time. Let me try again.

A swordsman faces an opponent. They are well matched. They have faced each other before, many times, and neither has been able to claim a decisive and unambiguous victory. Let us say they are, by any honest measure, equals. But on this day, the swordsman perceives something he has not perceived before. A gap. An opening. Not in the opponent's technique — the technique is superb, as it has always been — but in the opponent's *structure*. Something architectural. Something that was perhaps always there but became visible only because of conditions: the angle of light, the quality of attention, the particular silence of the room. Let us say that the opening is on the opponent's left side.

Now: the swordsman knows that if he strikes, he will win. He knows this with the certainty of a mathematician completing a proof. There is no question. The strike is available. The path is clear.

But the swordsman also knows — and here is where I lose my way, Fujimoto, here is where I have been losing my way for years — that this opening is not a *failing* of his opponent. It is a *feature*. It is woven into the way the man stands, the way he holds his weapon, the way he has built his life in his body. To exploit it would be to win. But to *name* it — even silently, even through the act of striking — would be to tell the man something about himself that he does not know and may not survive knowing. Because the flaw, if I may call it that, though I am no longer certain it is a flaw, is not a matter of footwork or grip. It is deeper. It is the place where the man's strength has been *compensating* for something, faithfully, invisibly, for an entire life. And to expose it would not improve him. It would only make him aware of the compensation, and the awareness would destroy the compensation, and the man would be left standing in his own body like a stranger.

So: does the swordsman strike? Does he refuse to strike? Does he walk away? And if he walks away, is he merciful, or is he a coward who has dressed his cowardice in the robes of mercy?

I am asking about the swordsman, of course. I am not asking about myself. I have traded my sword for a broom and my opponents for cedar planks and recalcitrant dust. But the swordsman interests me as a theoretical matter, and I find there are fewer people than I expected who can think clearly about violence and tenderness at the same time.

The wrist exercises — has Tanaka continued with them? I noticed, years ago, that his right wrist compensated for a slight inflexibility in the left. The exercises I described should address this over time, though time, as I am learning, addresses nothing so much as our willingness to wait for it.

With respect and, as always, gratitude for your patience with an old student of questions that may not have answers,

Hideo

*Editor's note: He was always better than I at hypotheticals.*

---

### Letter No. 14 (received April 1973)

Fujimoto,

I return to the swordsman. You will forgive me. Or you will not, and your forgiveness is not the currency I am attempting to earn.

I have come to believe the question is not whether silence is merciful. I have come to believe it is whether mercy can be a form of violence. Consider: the swordsman walks away. He does not strike. He does not name the opening. The opponent is left intact, undamaged, whole. But the opponent also knows something has happened. He knows because the swordsman's *refusal* to strike is itself a communication. A man who declines a winning blow has told his opponent more than a man who lands one. The strike would have said: *I am better.* The refusal says: *I have seen something in you that I will not speak.* And so the opponent is left not with a wound but with a question — and a question, I have come to believe, is a wound that does not have the decency to bleed.

Is silence the sword's sheath, or is it the blade itself?

I have been told by the abbot that my meditation is improving. He says I am learning to let thoughts pass without pursuing them. I was too ashamed to tell him that the one thought I cannot release is not a thought at all but a posture — a way of standing that I see behind my eyes, always, and that does not pass, and that I have never once, in twelve years, succeeded in not pursuing.

I am sending along a package of the dried persimmons we prepare here in autumn. They are ugly and very sweet.

Hideo
